reissueTells.claim: Fender’s ’59 reissue service drawing identifies control and main printed circuit boards. That differs from the original 5F6-A eyelet-board layout. The LTD specification lists a lacquered tweed pine cabinet, four Jensen P10R speakers and a rubber dogbone handle. Those present-day parts can resemble older designs, so their appearance alone doesn’t authenticate a 1959 amp.

The Bassman 60 service document identifies the much later PR421 model. Fender’s history also places the Bassman 20 and solid-state Compact after this guide’s cutoff. Read the complete rear model identification. Don’t place an unfamiliar Bassman into a 1960s group merely because it has black covering or a low serial number.

Ask a technician to photograph board construction if exterior labels leave the question open. A modern handwired replacement board or a complete replica can follow an old drawing closely. Hand assembly establishes how something was built, not when it was built. The same caution applies to an aged cabinet fitted with modern transformers.A new speaker inside an old cabinet is evidence of a changed speaker. It doesn’t, by itself, make the entire amplifier a reissue. Record the parts separately and look for agreement among the chassis, cabinet and component dates. If those groups disagree, describe the amp as needing further identification rather than forcing one date onto everything.
reissueTells.sourceNote: General identification reasoning; not a model-specific factory specification.

reissueTells.claim: The modern ’65 Super Reverb service diagram includes a combined printed circuit board carrying the controls and electronic components. The original AB763 uses an eyelet-board layout. Fender’s current specification also identifies four Jensen P10R speakers and a birch-plywood cabinet. New speakers can be fitted to an old amp, so confirm the chassis construction too.
reissueTells.sourceNote: Inline sources plus factory documents linked elsewhere on this page; general condition reasoning is separate from these specific model claims.

reissueTells.claim: A Tone Master Super Reverb has digital amplification and modern rear controls, including output attenuation and an XLR line output. The newer ’62 Super recreates brown cosmetics but lists two Celestion Custom ten-inch speakers. Its model documentation and modern components distinguish it from an original brown Super.

Handwiring doesn’t establish a vintage production date. A newly built tweed Super-style amp can use a traditional board and an old schematic. Ask for the maker’s identity, the chassis markings and the age of the major components. A replacement cabinet can also reproduce the outline of a V-front or narrow-panel amp.Use photographs of the front and rear together. A familiar grille may conceal a different chassis, while a modern replacement speaker can sit inside an otherwise old amplifier. The identification should explain both situations. Don’t open the chassis to investigate; a qualified technician can supply the board photographs needed for that comparison.
reissueTells.sourceNote: General identification reasoning; not a model-specific factory specification.

reissueTells.claim: Fender’s ’68 Custom manual names the channels Custom and Vintage. It specifies two Celestion TEN 30 speakers and reverb and tremolo on both channels. Those labels differ from the original Normal/Vibrato arrangement. The manual’s rear diagram also shows a detachable IEC power connection. These are practical clues before any chassis inspection.

The 1995 Custom Vibrolux service manual documents printed circuit-board construction and cream control knobs. That is a later product with a familiar name. The original AA964 drawing uses an eyelet-board layout. A technician can compare the construction when the rear identification or cabinet has been changed.
reissueTells.sourceNote: Inline sources plus factory documents linked elsewhere on this page; general condition reasoning is separate from these specific model claims.

reissueTells.claim: Some modern components deliberately reproduce older appearances. Fender’s ’68 Custom documentation even names Schumacher transformers, so a familiar transformer maker alone cannot establish a 1960s date. Read the full markings and identify the model as a whole. A speaker brand is useful evidence only when its actual model and production period are considered.A handwired replica can also follow an early Vibrolux circuit. Handwiring is a construction method, not an age test. Conversely, replacement speakers in an original amp don’t automatically make it a modern reissue. Separate the chassis identity from the age and condition of each replaceable component.The period all-transistor Vibrolux Reverb is another possible source of confusion. Its factory manual shows an angled control arrangement and identifies solid-state construction. It shouldn’t be confused with a tube amp that merely has diode rectification. The tube specifications below apply only to the named tube circuits.
reissueTells.sourceNote: Inline sources plus factory documents linked elsewhere on this page; general condition reasoning is separate from these specific model claims.

reissueTells.claim: Fender’s ’57 Custom specification describes a handwired 5F1 with a Weber eight-inch speaker and a 12AY7 preamp tube. Its modern manufacture shows why handwiring alone is insufficient. Fender’s Champ history identifies the EC Vibro-Champ by its EC grille badge, added tremolo-speed control and output attenuator. The original 5F1 has neither tremolo control nor attenuator.

The modern Champion 600 introduced in 2007 closely copies the earlier two-tone appearance. Fender’s history identifies its revised preamp and internal speaker-output jack. The ’68 Custom Vibro Champ Reverb is easier to distinguish: it has a ten-inch Celestion TEN 30 and digital hall reverb. A reverb control and larger stock speaker don’t match an original silverface Vibro Champ.
reissueTells.sourceNote: Inline sources plus factory documents linked elsewhere on this page; general condition reasoning is separate from these specific model claims.

reissueTells.claim: Read any rear product label and compare the entire amplifier with the documentation for that exact model. A replacement label or recovered cabinet can make the outside less conclusive. Have a technician document the board, transformers and tube sockets if the identification remains uncertain. Modern vintage-style components should be evaluated by their actual markings.The XD and X2 families add modern voicing or effects controls and fall outside this original-amp guide. Rivera-era Champ II and Super Champ models are also later exclusions. The familiar Champ name was used for several different products, so it shouldn’t be treated as a continuous specification from the 1940s onward.A replaced speaker in an old Champ is a condition finding, not automatic evidence that the whole amp is new. The reverse is also true: fitting an old speaker into a newer reproduction doesn’t create an original vintage amplifier. Identify the chassis and cabinet, then record the age of the installed parts individually.

conflicts.decision: Use exactly 1948 to 1959 tweed, 1959 to 1963 blonde/brownface, 1963 to 1967 blackface, 1967 to 1980 silverface. Model-specific overlaps are explicit. Earliest V-front Super group begins in 1947; Champ silver change is 1968.

conflicts.conflict: VG-AMP-0052 describes a different end date from the live house reference.
conflicts.decision: User explicitly requires the live dating page’s about-1970 rule and A=1951 mapping. No serial dating.

conflicts.conflict: Book page 461 lists 1972 to 1976, but the verified factory Bassman 60 document identifies 1999 PR421.
conflicts.decision: Omit the disputed row. Keep its frozen baseline and adjustment privately. Do not reuse 1999 specifications for an alleged 1970s amp.

conflicts.conflict: Book page 470 labels 35 watts; the period Fender manual states 42 watts RMS.
conflicts.decision: Omit that value row pending reconciliation. Preserve its exact original row privately; describe only identifying construction on the authentication page.

conflicts.conflict: Book page 461 prices a 2x12 set; Fender’s historical account describes a 2x15 combination.
conflicts.decision: Retain the book’s exact priced configuration. Authentication copy says actual cabinet pairings varied and requires an inventory; no 2x15 value invented.

conflicts.conflict: Book groups 1978 to 1983 and describes 4x10; Fender history describes the high-power continuation of the 4x12 Bassman 100.
conflicts.decision: No value row because the source group crosses 1980. Factory-authentication information covers pre-1981 examples only.

conflicts.conflict: Book prices 50 watts for 1972 to 1980 and a 70-watt group in 1981 to 1982. The later factory drawing is labeled 70 watts and includes 1977 revision dates; its mirror filename misleadingly says 75w.
conflicts.decision: Public value row retains exact book group. Later unmatched version gets individual appraisal. Authentication follows 70-watt factory title, no 75-watt claim.

conflicts.conflict: Book page 468 labels its 1956 to 1957 6V6 entry 5E4. The verified schematic title is 5E4-A, with a 1955 drawing code.
conflicts.decision: Value row preserves book’s group. Technical page calls the drawing 5E4-A and does not turn its drawing date into a claimed individual production date. Exact 6V6 output rating is left unasserted.

conflicts.topic: Super Reverb master-volume and high-power dates
conflicts.conflict: Book and field records place control and rating changes in different year groups. Factory 45-watt and 70-watt drawings both show master-volume/pull controls.
conflicts.decision: Show both electrical designs; avoid assigning power by the knob or imposing a disputed exact transition year. Values retain source year groups.

conflicts.conflict: Some field entries list only a generic preamp tube rather than every tube, and the brown Vibrolux field record differs from the 6G11-A drawing.
conflicts.decision: Use full factory sets: 6G11-A two 7025 plus two 12AX7; 6G4-A four 7025 plus two 12AX7; Bassman 100/135 two 7025 plus one 12AT7. Schematic labels were inspected visually.

Bassman 6G6-B and Super Reverb AB763 chart printing is legible, but the date letters remain undecoded. Use only verified NC and IB readings. Joe explicitly confirmed the pictured Super Reverb as a 1965 on November 3, 2026; that owner identification supersedes the earlier broad archive range without inventing a chart-stamp reading.
